| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -21.1% at 31x; -37.4% at 24.6x | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield above 5%; forward P/E above 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Cash quality and inventory | Medium, 30-50% | FCF -$1.9bn to $123.2bn, 41.2x; inventory -$3.3bn | Low | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | Other-liabilities note; inventory $11.1bn | Underwrite the $123.2bn case | S6, S5, S17 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | No named successor; director exits | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S141, S11 |

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in Q1 2026 versus 2025; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts Q4 DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin, 200bp below the 48% top of the base range, takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to $9.27 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $269 — the entry price, not a discount. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.3x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, with the DOJ's cross-appeal, stays live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit. A 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14 on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across 2.5bn devices would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells $1,199 handsets is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in H2 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds India — 25% of iPhones, incentives expired 2026-03-31, costs above China's — and Section 301 duties replacing the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk, and the entry ladder assumes the base EPS

At 39.3x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.5x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.8-41.4x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,071.2bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.1%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 37.4%. Each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF 15-18%; the ten-year is 4.93% against a 7.0% implied return. A 30% revenue fall leaves $326.8bn; on the 43.0% nine-month incremental operating margin it leaves $94.6bn of operating income and $5.4 of EPS, but that is an up-cycle margin. On the FY2021-FY2025 average gross margin of 44.5%, with $72.3bn of operating expense held flat, gross profit is $145.3bn, operating income $73.0bn and EPS $4.10 at the 17.3% tax rate on 14.75bn diluted shares — a 58% decremental margin, not 43%; a 10% cost cut lifts EPS to $4.50, and the FY2016-FY2025 average margin of 41.4% gives $3.54. At 29x that is $103-131, at or below the $133 DCF bear. A market 50% smaller is revenue 35% lower and EPS $3.51, $70-88 at 20-25x. Free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn, 56.9-59.1x, covering the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not. The entry ladder is the same single-point bet: 0.75-1.0% at $270 is 27.6x only on FY2027 EPS of $9.79. A 46% gross margin takes EPS to $9.27 and $270 to 29.1x; a search cut of 12.9% takes $9.79 to $8.53 and, with the margin, to $8.07, so $270 becomes 31.7x to 33.5x against the 31.0x four-year mean and $245 becomes 28.7x to 30.4x. The same 27.6x is $223-235 on $8.07-8.53. The ladder needs a condition, not a new number: $270 only if the 2026-11-02 guide holds FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and December gross margin at 47%; otherwise the first tranche belongs at $235 and the second at $210, with the 5% cap unchanged. [S10, S97, S6, S5, S151, S70]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors. Cook is Executive Chair and Ternus CEO under a nine-director board. Srouji's 2025-12-06 departure report is superseded by his 2026-04-20 promotion to Chief Hardware Officer with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. Cash quality is smaller than it looked: the $13,531M non-current liability build against $13,270M of gross intangibles added reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M current-liability fall it is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M line; if unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, inside the $122.6-127.3bn band. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence is the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough and EPS at $9.27 or better. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]

## Investment Potential & Thesis

Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base and services annuity are real, and FY2026 is strong: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,072bn market capitalisation, 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.7 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S156].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the DCF bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap; the base rate is modest, with revenue compounding 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value; this report sees 18% overvaluation: retail aggregator targets are $338-355, unverified, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price, and the recommendation rests on that weighted value and the $284 base case, not on the bull. The scenario bull ($357, 25%) — distinct from the $277 DCF bull above — assumes the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate: 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 without a break-up: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the settlement did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.3x against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash; the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. The first tranche of 0.75-1.0% is $270 only on a condition: the 2026-11-02 guide must hold FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and gross margin at 47%. At 27.6 times, $270 is a discount only on the $9.79 base EPS; on $9.27 it is 29.1 times, and on $8.07-8.53, after a 12.9% search-payment cut, 31.7-33.5 times, above the 31.0x mean. Those lower cases imply $223-235, so if the guide holds the second tranche is $245; if it fails the first moves to $235 and the second to $210. The position reaches its 5% cap below $225 or if FY2027 EPS growth tracks above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the ladder prices the EPS bridge rather than a single point. The counter-evidence is the stock's own record: 27.5% in the twelve months to 30 October 2026; a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, neither of which the register holds. Sell above 45 times forward earnings ($440), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

## Exit Strategy Analysis

Apple's only exit is the public market and its own buyback, and at $344.63 the shares already discount the scenario bull. No peer is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,071.2bn market value (14,715m diluted shares at $344.63) — so realisation depends on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and gross buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.3x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and sell at $440 and above — 45x FY2027E EPS of $9.79 — not at the $357 scenario bull [S7, S11, S6, S97].

Liquidity is not the constraint: Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any long-only position, so the exit is never closed. The intended holding period is three years. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds, and in a broad de-rating they mark the multiple down together.

Two things follow. The operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% the shares have just delivered in twelve months. And the buyback does much of the work, buying a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar at 39.3x, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so it supports the price without creating value at this level. An investor paying 39.3x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.3x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.1% of the price, or 7.6% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount on post-2035 cash flows is higher than at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

The sell discipline follows from that table, which assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. It also follows from the scenario range: at $344.63 the shares are 97% of the $357 scenario bull at 35x FY2027E EPS of $10.20 and 121% of the $284 scenario base at 29x, while the DCF bull at an 8.5% discount rate is $277, 20% below the market. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth runs above 12% rather than the 9.9% consensus assumes for iPhone revenue. At $270 the 9.9% return assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45; a 6% lower path cuts it to 7.7%, and the $9.19-10.08 FY2027 band at 27.6x gives a $254-278 entry around that $270 midpoint. I would raise the entry price on services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. I would sell if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10% or gross margin below 47%, or if a services structure removes the search payment. A sale at 45x forward, $440, 23.2% above the bull's $357 and 27.7% above the price, is a multiple extreme, not a value target — a holder sells into a melt-up, a buyer waits for a de-rating. The 45x sits above the table's range because it is a melt-up exit, not a base case [S71, S72, S6, S7, S97].

The bear case sets the drawdown to expect, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241-243: a reversion to Apple's 2022 multiple of 24.6x on FY2027E earnings gives $241, and the $243.42 low the shares printed within the past twelve months is $243. That is a 30% drawdown. The DCF bear of $133 is a different animal — gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a 9.5% discount rate together — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 2.1% of the shares at $270 and 2.3% at $240, against 1.6% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The discipline has been wrong before. Apple has compounded while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That argues for modest size and buying weakness, not to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on multiple reversion. The open question is the Google payment's share of services revenue and when the appeal is decided; neither is publicly disclosed; both set the floor under the services multiple.

## ESG Assessment

Apple's regulatory exposure, not its ESG record, is what can change a long-only case. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn and Services revenue $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin, so App Store commissions and the Google default-search payment sit inside the profit pool carrying the premium multiple [S5]. Fines are not the mechanism; remedies and fee schedules are. Bear case: a 10-15% operating-income tail from losing or repricing search placement and a structurally lower App Store take rate over 2026-2028. A dollar of commission or default rent carries almost no marginal cost, so losing it hits operating income faster than revenue.

### The EU fine is small; the fee schedule is not

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation, 0.1% of FY2025 net sales. The material part is the fee schedule: from 2026-10-01 Apple's unified EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase (down from 30%), 20% on alternative payments, 15% on link-outs and 5% on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web. Apple calls the terms a settlement; EU developer groups contest them. Apple does not disclose EU App Store revenue; at a 75.4% Services margin, each $1bn of commission lost equals $0.75bn of gross profit, and the take rate falls permanently [S78, S77, S5].

### The $20 billion Google payment is the largest policy-sensitive cash flow

Apple does not disclose the Google default-search payment, but the US v. Google trial record put it at $20bn in 2022, or 36% of Google's Safari search revenue: a litigated estimate, not an Apple disclosure. That is 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue and, if near-pure margin, 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's final judgment of 2025-12-05 preserved non-exclusive payments, banned exclusivity and capped default deals at 12 months; the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026 seeking a payment ban. A lower negotiated rate is more likely than zero, because the payment is worth more as Apple profit than as Google cost; either way it compresses Services growth, and an appellate decision is likely in 2027 [S80, S76, S5].

### US courts are already narrowing the App Store take rate

On 2025-12-11 the Ninth Circuit affirmed that Apple willfully violated the Epic injunction, upheld the steering remedy and limited any fee on linked transactions to Apple's costs; the Supreme Court granted certiorari on 2026-06-30. The DOJ and 16 states and DC have sued Apple for monopolization of "performance smartphones" and "smartphones" since 2024-03-21, seeking equitable relief, not damages; pre-trial litigation has no trial date in Apple's 2026 filings. A willful-violation finding raises the odds of stricter remedies and weakens management's "substantial defenses" posture. US courts can reset App Store economics before the DOJ case reaches trial [S79, S81, S6].

### Tariffs have flipped from cost to refund, not to a new margin level

Q3 FY2026 revenue was $109.4bn and gross margin 50.1%, including 2 percentage points from tariff refunds; EPS of $2.02 included $0.11 from refunds. The underlying margin is 48.1%, against 46.9% for FY2025, when products gross margin fell on tariff costs. The refund follows the Supreme Court's 2026-02-20 ruling striking down certain IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 semiconductor results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products, but Section 301 duties have since been imposed and more remain possible. For valuation, normalise the margin rather than extrapolate the refund: underwrite 47-48%, not 50% [S17, S5, S6].

### Governance is sound, but the chair is now the former CEO

Governance is not the discount, but the structure changed on 2026-09-01: Tim Cook became Executive Chair, John Ternus became CEO and a ninth director, and Arthur Levinson became Lead Independent Director. The chair is the former CEO, not independent; the independent check now rests on the lead director. The board also waived its guideline against re-election after age 75 for Levinson (75) and Audit Chair Ron Sugar (77), both re-elected in 2026, so refreshment lags the rule. Offsetting that, there is no dual-class stock, four of the 2026 directors were women, the Audit Committee owns privacy and cybersecurity, related-party transactions above $120,000 need its approval, and the 2026 executive-pay vote passed. The gaps are labour and disclosure: 166,000 employees at 2025-09-27, a 10-K concession that supplier code violations "occur from time to time", and no audit metrics; climate claims are unverified. None has changed demand, so ESG is a tail-risk and discount-rate input, not a revenue driver [S56, S11, S138].

Until then, price the tail in the discount rate and a Services multiple below the market's implied assumptions.

## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation

The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.7 times forward (FactSet, 2026-10-23) and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S156]. The DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212, the DCF bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the scenario bull is $357 at 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20; the recommendation rests on the $284 base case and the 25/50/25 weighted $291.5, not on either bull, because the market price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. The retail aggregator targets of $338-355, unverified, offer flat to +3%, so there is no analyst catalyst to close the gap either.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 41.2 times.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. The score table below carries the figures and their sources.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter, and the table below carries the mechanics. At the current price the probability-weighted return across the three scenarios is negative, so the Kelly fraction is zero. At $270 the memo's own 25/50/25 outcomes — bull $357 (+32%), base $284 (+5%), bear $241 (-11%) — produce an expected log-growth optimum near 5x the fund, so full Kelly is unusable for a long-only fund; the 5% cap is a risk limit, not a Kelly fraction, and the 0.75-1.0% first tranche rising to 2.5-3.0% is deliberately a small fraction of it. The market regime reinforces patience: an elevated volatility percentile, a ten-year yield at 4.93% and a month of technology underperformance against the index are the profile the regime playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10, S6, S7]. The open diligence is the FY2026 10-K detail on working capital and intangibles, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, and the appellate outcome on the search payment.

1. Do not own Apple at $344.63: the base case is $284 (-18%) and the probability-weighted value $292, so the price, not the franchise, is the problem [S6, S7].
2. The two facts that would change the call are a 46% gross margin, which takes fair value to $270 at 29 times, and a D.C. Circuit ban on the search payment, which removes 12.9% of EPS [S17, S99, S76].
3. Stage the entry: a conditional 0.75-1.0% at $270 only if the 2026-11-02 guide holds FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and gross margin at 47%; otherwise $235, a second tranche at $245 or $210, the 5% cap below $225, and a maximum loss of 1.5% of the fund at the cap [S6, S7].
